# 7. The console

<!-- Generated by tools/generate-docs.lisp from docs/manual/chapters.lisp,
     docs/manual/introduction.md and the examples: do not edit by hand. -->

The console library, (require 'console), writes styled text with the colors a
terminal has and none to a pipe, measures and wraps it in cells, reads keys as
events, lays text out in rules, panels, tables and trees, asks questions and
offers choices, and tests what a program draws on a pretend terminal.

## Styled text, measured and wrapped, and a screen to test it on

(require 'console) brings in the console library (specs/29-console.md), in
the manner of .NET's Spectre.Console. Markup such as "[bold green]done[/]"
writes its text in its styles, with the colors the terminal has: to a pipe or
a file there are none, so this example's output is plain text. Text is
measured in cells, as a terminal shows it, and wrapped at the console's width.

with-test-console runs a piece of a program against a pretend terminal of a
given size, and answers its screen: the text on it, and the style of each
cell. That is how a program that draws on a terminal is tested without one.
Inside it, a program's output goes to that screen; the keys it reads come
from a list, and arrive as events.

`examples/console.lisp`:

```scheme
(require 'console)

(print-markup-line "[bold green]done[/] in [blue]3 s[/], with [[brackets]] shown as they are")
(with-console '(width 30)
  (lambda () (render "Text is wrapped at the console's width, here thirty cells, at its spaces.")))
(display (list (text-width "abc") (text-width "漢字"))) (newline)

;; a screen 12 cells wide: what was drawn, and how
(define screen
  (with-test-console '(width 12 height 4)
    (lambda () (print-markup-line "[red on white]warning[/] two") (render "wraps at twelve cells"))))
(display (screen-text screen)) (newline)
(display (style-foreground (cdr (screen-cell screen 1 1)))) (newline)

;; keys, as a terminal would send them, read as events
(define keys '())
(with-test-console '(events (down down enter (ctrl #\c)))
  (lambda ()
    (let loop ()
      (let ((e (read-event)))
        (if (not (eq? (event-kind e) 'eof))
            (begin (set! keys (cons (list (or (event-key e) (event-char e)) (event-modifiers e)) keys))
                   (loop)))))))
(for-each (lambda (k) (write k) (newline)) (reverse keys))
```

Its output:

```text
done in 3 s, with [brackets] shown as they are
Text is wrapped at the
console's width, here thirty
cells, at its spaces.
(3 4)
warning two
wraps at
twelve cells
red
(down ())
(down ())
(enter ())
(#\c (ctrl))
```

## Rules, panels, tables and trees

A renderable is a value: (render x) writes it at the console's width. rule
draws a titled line, panel a box, table a grid of cells with headers, tree a
label with branches, and columns lays items side by side. Options follow as
pairs of a name and a value, since cog-lisp has no keyword arguments.

Anything renders: text, markup's styled text, any value, and the renderables
themselves, so a table's cell can hold a panel. A table too wide for the
console shrinks, wrapping its cells at their spaces. Without Unicode, the
borders are drawn in ASCII.

`examples/console-renderables.lisp`:

```scheme
(require 'console)

(with-console '(width 44)
  (lambda ()
    (render (rule "Inventory"))
    (let ((t (table 'columns (list "Item" (table-column "Qty" 'align 'right) "Note") 'title "Stock")))
      (table-add-row! t "apples" 12 "")
      (table-add-row! t "figs" 3 (markup "[red]low: order more before the weekend[/]"))
      (render t))
    (render (panel "Two items, fifteen in all." 'header "Summary" 'border 'rounded))
    (render (tree "warehouse" (tree "shelf a" "apples") (tree "shelf b" "figs")))
    (render (columns '("north" "south" "east" "west")))))

(with-console '(width 30 unicode? #f)
  (lambda () (render (panel "ASCII, for a console without Unicode"))))
```

Its output:

```text
──────────────── Inventory ─────────────────
                   Stock
┌────────┬─────┬───────────────────────────┐
│ Item   │ Qty │ Note                      │
├────────┼─────┼───────────────────────────┤
│ apples │  12 │                           │
│ figs   │   3 │ low: order more before    │
│        │     │ the weekend               │
└────────┴─────┴───────────────────────────┘
╭─ Summary ──────────────────╮
│ Two items, fifteen in all. │
╰────────────────────────────╯
warehouse
├── shelf a
│   └── apples
└── shelf b
    └── figs
north  south  east  west
+----------------------------+
| ASCII, for a console       |
| without Unicode            |
+----------------------------+
```

## Asking, confirming and choosing

ask reads an answer, with a default, a check (validate) and secret typing;
confirm a yes or no; choose one item from a list with the arrow keys and
Enter, and choose-many several, Space marking each. On a terminal they read
keys; Ctrl+C or Escape cancels, a condition prompt-cancelled? tells, and the
terminal is always left as it was. confirm answers on y or n alone; an Enter
pressed after it is an empty line for the next read, on Windows and Linux.

Without a terminal, when the input is piped or a file, each reads a line
instead: the answer, or an item's number or name. So a program that asks can
be run from a script. Here a test console stands in for both: once with keys,
once with lines of input, and its screen shows what the person would see. To
try a whole program at a real terminal without a person, the console driver,
tools/console_driver.py, types at it from a script (docs/mcp.md).

`examples/console-prompts.lisp`:

```scheme
(require 'console)

;; with keys: a, b, backspace, c, Enter; then down, down, Enter
(define answers '())
(define screen
  (with-test-console '(width 40 events ("ab" backspace "c" enter down down enter))
    (lambda ()
      (set! answers (list (ask "Your name?") (choose "Favorite color" '(red green blue)))))))
(write answers) (newline)
(display (screen-text screen)) (newline) (newline)

;; with lines of input, as from a pipe: a number is the item at that place
(define piped
  (with-test-console '(width 40 input "\nAnn\nyes\n2\n")
    (lambda ()
      (set! answers (list (ask "Your name?" 'default "Bo")
                          (ask "Your name?")
                          (confirm "Continue?")
                          (choose "Size" '(small medium large)))))))
(write answers) (newline)
(display (screen-text piped)) (newline)
```

Its output:

```text
("ac" blue)
Your name? ac
Favorite color blue

("Bo" "Ann" #t medium)
Your name? (Bo)
Your name?
Continue? [y/n]
Size
  1. small
  2. medium
  3. large
?
```
